questions.question: What is the difference between a Node.js core module, a locally created module, and a third-party npm package?
questions.answer: A core module ships built into Node.js itself — `fs`, `http`, `path`, `crypto`, etc. — requiring no installation; you `require('node:fs')` (the `node:` prefix is the modern, recommended form) and it's always available regardless of what's in `node_modules`. A locally created module is a file you write yourself within your project — e.g., `./utils/formatDate.js` — and reference by relative or absolute path (`require('./utils/formatDate')`), used to organize your own application code into reusable pieces. A third-party npm package is code written by someone else, published to the npm registry, installed into your project's `node_modules` via `npm install`, and referenced by its package name (`require('lodash')`) — Node's module resolution algorithm walks up the directory tree looking for a matching folder under `node_modules` when the specifier isn't a relative path and isn't a recognized core module name.

questions.question: What is nvm (Node Version Manager), and why would a development team use it?
questions.answer: nvm is a command-line tool for installing and switching between multiple Node.js versions on the same machine, without needing to uninstall/reinstall Node each time you switch projects. A team uses it because different projects (or different branches, or a legacy service versus a new one) often target different Node.js LTS versions, and a developer moving between them needs to match each project's expected runtime exactly to avoid version-specific bugs. In practice, teams commit a `.nvmrc` file to the repo root specifying the required version, so anyone running `nvm use` in that directory automatically switches to the correct version — this keeps local development version-consistent with CI and production without manual coordination. It's worth noting nvm only manages the Node runtime version; it has nothing to do with npm package versions, which are handled separately by `package.json`/`package-lock.json`.

questions.question: How do you access command-line arguments passed to a Node.js script?
questions.answer: Node.js populates the global `process.argv` array with the arguments the process was launched with. Per the official docs, index `0` is the path to the Node executable itself, index `1` is the path to the script being run, and everything from index `2` onward is what the user actually typed after the script name — so the standard pattern is `process.argv.slice(2)` to get just the user-supplied arguments. For example, running `node deploy.js --env=production --force` gives `process.argv = ['/usr/local/bin/node', '/path/deploy.js', '--env=production', '--force']`. For simple positional arguments, working with the sliced array directly is fine; for anything with named flags, short aliases, or boolean switches, Node's built-in `node:util` module now ships a stable `parseArgs()` function (stable since Node 20) that takes an options schema and returns structured `{ values, positionals }`, avoiding the need for a third-party CLI-parsing library like `yargs` or `commander` for straightforward cases.

questions.question: What is the os module used for in Node.js?
questions.answer: The `node:os` core module provides information about, and interacts with, the underlying operating system the Node.js process is running on — without needing any external package. Common uses: `os.platform()` and `os.type()` to detect the OS (e.g., for cross-platform path handling or conditional logic), `os.cpus()` to get the number and details of logical CPU cores (frequently used to decide how many `cluster` workers to fork, often combined with `os.availableParallelism()` in newer Node versions), `os.totalmem()`/`os.freemem()` for memory diagnostics, `os.hostname()`, and `os.homedir()`/`os.tmpdir()` for locating standard user/system directories. It's a low-level, informational module — it doesn't let you spawn OS processes (that's `child_process`) or manage the filesystem in depth (that's `fs`); it's specifically for querying facts about the host environment.

questions.question: What are unit tests, integration tests, and end-to-end tests, and how do they differ?
questions.answer: A unit test verifies a single, isolated piece of logic — one function, one class method — in isolation from its real dependencies, typically mocking out anything external (a database call, another module) so the test is fast and only fails when that specific unit's logic is wrong. An integration test verifies that multiple units work correctly together — e.g., that a service function correctly reads from and writes to a real (test) database, or that an Express route handler correctly wires together validation, business logic, and a data layer — catching bugs at the seams between components that unit tests, with everything mocked, would miss. An end-to-end (E2E) test exercises the whole system the way a real user or client would — spinning up the actual running application (or a close approximation) and making real HTTP requests against it, verifying complete user flows work correctly across every layer, including things like actual network calls and real infrastructure. The trade-off across all three is speed and confidence versus cost: unit tests are fast and cheap to write but give the least end-to-end confidence; E2E tests give the most realistic confidence but are slower, more brittle, and more expensive to maintain — which is why most teams follow a 'testing pyramid' with many unit tests, fewer integration tests, and a small number of E2E tests.

questions.question: What is the crypto module used for in Node.js, and what is one common use case?
questions.answer: The `node:crypto` core module provides cryptographic functionality — hashing, HMAC, encryption/decryption, digital signatures, and secure random value generation — built on OpenSSL, without needing a third-party library for common cryptographic primitives. A very common use case is generating a secure random token, e.g. for password-reset links or API keys: `crypto.randomBytes(32).toString('hex')` produces a cryptographically strong random string, which is important because `Math.random()` is not cryptographically secure and must never be used for anything security-sensitive (tokens, session ids, keys). Other frequent uses include hashing data with `crypto.createHash('sha256')` (for non-password use cases like generating a checksum or an ETag — note that for passwords specifically, a purpose-built, slow, salted algorithm like bcrypt or argon2 should be used instead of a fast general-purpose hash like SHA-256, precisely because fast hashes make brute-forcing easier) and HMAC signing (`crypto.createHmac`) for verifying webhook payload authenticity.

questions.question: What is the difference between the GET, POST, PUT, and DELETE HTTP methods in a REST API?
questions.answer: These are the core HTTP verbs REST APIs map onto CRUD operations. `GET` retrieves a resource (or collection) and should be safe and idempotent — it must not have side effects, and calling it repeatedly returns the same result (barring underlying data changes). `POST` creates a new resource (or triggers a non-idempotent action) — calling it twice with the same body typically creates two separate resources, which is why `POST` is not idempotent by definition. `PUT` replaces an existing resource entirely with the payload provided, and is idempotent — sending the same `PUT` request multiple times leaves the resource in the same end state. `DELETE` removes a resource, and is also considered idempotent — deleting an already-deleted resource is generally treated as a no-op success (or a `404`, depending on API design), rather than an error each time. A well-designed REST API also uses status codes consistently with these semantics: `200`/`201` for successful `GET`/`POST`, `204 No Content` often for successful `DELETE`, and appropriate `4xx` codes when a request violates these expectations.

questions.question: What is a WebSocket connection, and how does it differ from a regular HTTP request?
questions.answer: A regular HTTP request is a one-shot request/response cycle: the client opens a connection, sends a request, gets one response, and (for a simple request) the exchange is done — real-time updates require the client to poll repeatedly. A WebSocket connection starts as a normal HTTP request but includes an `Upgrade: websocket` header; if the server agrees, the connection is upgraded (via the HTTP/1.1 Upgrade mechanism) into a persistent, full-duplex TCP connection that stays open, over which either side can send messages to the other at any time, without the overhead of a new HTTP request/response handshake for every message. This makes WebSockets well-suited for real-time, bidirectional use cases — chat applications, live notifications, collaborative editing, live dashboards — where the server needs to push data to the client without waiting to be asked. In Node.js, the `ws` library or Socket.IO (which adds automatic reconnection, room/broadcast abstractions, and fallback transports on top of raw WebSockets) are the common tools for building a WebSocket server.

questions.question: What is the purpose of a linter like ESLint in a Node.js project?
questions.answer: ESLint statically analyzes your source code (without running it) to catch problems before they reach runtime or code review: likely bugs (using an undeclared variable, unreachable code, a missing `await`), stylistic inconsistencies (quote style, indentation, semicolon usage — though this overlaps with a formatter like Prettier), and enforcement of team- or framework-specific best practices via configurable rule sets (e.g., disallowing `console.log` in committed code, requiring error handling in Promise chains). It's typically wired into a project via a config file (`.eslintrc` or the newer flat `eslint.config.js`), run manually (`npx eslint .`), on save in an editor, and — critically for a team — enforced in CI so a pull request with lint violations fails the build rather than relying on manual review to catch style/quality issues. The main value proposition in an interview answer is consistency and early bug detection at effectively zero runtime cost, since it runs entirely at development/CI time.

questions.question: How would you test an Express API using Jest and Supertest?
questions.answer: Supertest lets you make HTTP-like requests directly against your Express `app` object in-process — no need to actually bind to a network port — and chain assertions on the response. A typical setup: export your configured Express `app` (without calling `.listen()` in the testable module, so tests can import it directly), then in the test file: `const request = require('supertest'); const app = require('../app'); test('GET /users/:id returns the user', async () => { const res = await request(app).get('/users/1'); expect(res.statusCode).toBe(200); expect(res.body).toMatchObject({ id: 1 }); });`. Jest provides the test runner, assertion library (`expect`), and mocking utilities around this — you'd typically also mock the database layer (or point at an isolated test database) so tests are deterministic and don't depend on external state, and use `beforeEach`/`afterEach` hooks to reset that state between tests. This combination (Jest + Supertest) is the standard pattern for integration-testing Express routes because it exercises the real middleware stack, routing, and serialization logic without the overhead of spinning up an actual server and making real network calls.

questions.question: How do you mock a module or function in Jest, and when would you use jest.spyOn() versus jest.mock()?
questions.answer: `jest.mock('./emailService')` replaces an entire module with an auto-mocked (or manually defined) version for the duration of the test file — every export becomes a mock function by default — which is the right tool when you want to fully isolate the unit under test from a dependency it imports, e.g., preventing a real email from being sent during a test of the signup flow. `jest.spyOn(object, 'methodName')` instead wraps a specific method on an existing object/module with a mock, while (by default) still calling through to the real implementation unless you also call `.mockImplementation()` on it — this is useful when you want to observe or assert how a function was called (arguments, call count) without necessarily replacing its behavior, or when you only want to mock one method of a module and leave the rest of its real behavior intact. A common pattern: `jest.spyOn(logger, 'error').mockImplementation(() => {});` to silence and assert on error logging during a test without mocking the entire logger module. Both approaches are cleaned up with `jest.restoreAllMocks()` (for spies) or reset between tests via Jest's config (`clearMocks`/`restoreMocks`) so mock state from one test doesn't leak into the next.

questions.question: What is code coverage, and which coverage metrics does a tool like Jest report?
questions.answer: Code coverage measures how much of your source code was actually executed while running your test suite, expressed as a percentage — it's a proxy for how thoroughly tested your code is, though a high percentage doesn't guarantee your tests actually assert the right things (you can execute a line without meaningfully testing its behavior). Jest, via Istanbul under the hood, reports four standard metrics when run with `--coverage`: statements (percentage of executable statements run), branches (percentage of conditional branches — both sides of an `if`/`else`, each case of a `switch` — that were exercised), functions (percentage of declared functions that were called at least once), and lines (percentage of physical lines of code executed). Branch coverage is generally considered the most meaningful of the four for catching untested logic paths, since a line can be 'covered' while only one of its possible branches was ever actually exercised (e.g., an `if` that was always true in tests, never false). Teams often set a minimum coverage threshold in CI (e.g., 80%) to fail a build that drops below it, though chasing 100% coverage as a goal in itself is generally considered a poor use of effort compared to focusing tests on business-critical or error-prone code paths.

questions.question: What is the difference between Mocha and Jest as testing frameworks for Node.js?
questions.answer: Mocha is a test runner only — it provides the `describe`/`it` structure and hooks (`before`, `beforeEach`, etc.) but deliberately doesn't ship an assertion library or mocking framework, so you pair it with separate libraries (commonly Chai for assertions, Sinon for spies/mocks/stubs), giving you flexibility to mix and match tools but requiring more setup and configuration decisions upfront. Jest is a more batteries-included, all-in-one framework: it bundles its own assertion library (`expect`), built-in mocking (`jest.mock`, `jest.fn`), snapshot testing, and code coverage reporting (via Istanbul) with zero additional configuration needed to get started, and it also parallelizes test files across worker processes by default for speed. In practice, Jest has become the more common default for new Node.js/JavaScript projects specifically because of that lower setup friction and its strong ecosystem integration with frontend frameworks (it's also the default for Create React App and many others), while Mocha remains popular in some existing codebases and among teams who specifically want to choose their own assertion/mocking libraries rather than use an opinionated bundle. It's also worth mentioning Node.js now ships a built-in `node:test` module as a lighter-weight, dependency-free alternative to either.

questions.question: How would you test asynchronous code that returns a Promise or uses async/await?
questions.answer: In Jest, the key rule is to make the test function itself `async` and `await` the code under test, or `return` the Promise it produces — if you forget this, the test can finish and report as passing before the async assertion inside it has even run, silently hiding failures. Correct pattern: `test('fetches the user', async () => { const user = await getUser(1); expect(user.name).toBe('Alice'); });` — Jest waits for the returned/awaited promise chain to settle before deciding pass/fail. To test that an async function correctly rejects/throws, use `await expect(someAsyncCall()).rejects.toThrow('Not found')` rather than wrapping in a manual `try/catch` with a `fail()` call in the `catch`, since that pattern is easy to get wrong (e.g., forgetting to actually fail the test if no error was thrown). For code involving timers (`setTimeout`, `setInterval`), Jest's fake timers (`jest.useFakeTimers()` plus `jest.advanceTimersByTime()`) let you deterministically fast-forward virtual time instead of making tests actually wait in real time, which keeps the suite fast and avoids flakiness from real timing dependencies.

questions.question: How would you set up an isolated test database for integration tests in a Node.js application?
questions.answer: The goal is that integration tests run against a real database engine (so you're testing real query behavior, constraints, and transactions) while remaining fully isolated from development/production data and safely repeatable. The most robust modern approach is spinning up a throwaway database instance in a Docker container specifically for the test run (via `testcontainers` or a `docker-compose.test.yml`), so each CI run gets a completely clean instance with no shared state or cross-test pollution, then tearing it down after the suite finishes. A lighter-weight alternative for SQL databases is running migrations against a dedicated `myapp_test` database (never the same instance as dev/prod) and wrapping each test in a transaction that's rolled back at the end (`beforeEach` starts a transaction, `afterEach` rolls it back), which keeps tests fast since nothing is actually persisted between runs. Either way, critical practices are: never point tests at a database with real data, seed a known, minimal dataset before each test (or test file) rather than relying on incidental leftover state from a previous test, and keep the test database connection configuration entirely separate (a distinct connection string/env var) from development and production to eliminate any chance of a misconfigured test run touching real data.

questions.question: How do you securely hash and verify passwords in a Node.js application (e.g., with bcrypt)?
questions.answer: Never store plaintext passwords, and never use a fast general-purpose hash like MD5 or plain SHA-256 for passwords — those are designed to be fast, which makes them cheap to brute-force at scale with modern hardware (GPUs/ASICs). Instead use a purpose-built, deliberately slow, adaptive password-hashing algorithm like bcrypt (or argon2/scrypt), which bakes in both a random salt (so identical passwords don't produce identical hashes, defeating precomputed rainbow-table attacks) and a configurable work factor (cost) that can be increased over time as hardware gets faster. With the `bcrypt` npm package: on signup, `const hash = await bcrypt.hash(plainPassword, 12)` (12 is a commonly used cost factor, balancing security against login latency) — the resulting hash string already embeds the salt and cost factor, so you only need to store that one string. On login, you don't decrypt anything (bcrypt hashing is one-way) — you re-hash the submitted password the same way and let bcrypt do the comparison: `const isValid = await bcrypt.compare(submittedPassword, storedHash)`, which internally re-derives using the salt/cost embedded in `storedHash` and does a constant-time comparison to avoid leaking timing information about how much of the hash matched.

questions.question: What are common security vulnerabilities in Node.js/Express applications (e.g., XSS, insecure dependencies, injection), and how do you defend against them?
questions.answer: A few of the most common, recurring categories: Injection (SQL/NoSQL/command injection) — from building queries or shell commands by concatenating untrusted input — defended against with parameterized queries and never passing user input directly to `child_process.exec()` or a shell. Cross-Site Scripting (XSS) — untrusted input rendered into HTML/JS without escaping, letting an attacker run script in another user's browser — defended against by using a templating engine or frontend framework that auto-escapes output by default, and applying a strict Content-Security-Policy header. Insecure/outdated dependencies — a vulnerable transitive npm package pulled into your app without your knowledge — defended against by running `npm audit` (or a dedicated tool like Snyk/Dependabot) regularly in CI and keeping dependencies patched. Broken authentication/session handling — weak password policies, tokens that never expire, missing rate limiting on login — defended against with the practices already covered under password hashing, JWT expiry, and rate limiting. Sensitive data exposure — secrets committed to source control, verbose error messages leaking stack traces or internal paths to clients in production. Beyond these specific fixes, sane defaults come largely 'for free' from using Helmet (secure headers), validating all input, running the app as a non-root user, and keeping the dependency tree audited and minimal.

questions.question: How would you set secure HTTP headers in an Express app, and what does a middleware like Helmet do?
questions.answer: By default, Express (and Node's `http` module) doesn't add most of the security-relevant response headers browsers can use to enforce stricter protections, so you'd otherwise have to set each one manually via `res.setHeader()` on every response. The `helmet` middleware bundles a collection of smaller middleware functions, each setting one specific security header, and applies them all with a single line: `app.use(helmet())`. Among what it configures out of the box: `Strict-Transport-Security` (forces browsers to only connect over HTTPS for a specified duration, preventing protocol-downgrade attacks), `X-Content-Type-Options: nosniff` (stops browsers from MIME-sniffing a response away from its declared content type, which can prevent certain XSS vectors), `X-Frame-Options`/frame-ancestors (mitigates clickjacking by controlling whether your site can be embedded in an iframe), and a baseline `Content-Security-Policy`. It's still important to tune Helmet's defaults for your specific app (e.g., CSP often needs to be customized to actually allow your legitimate scripts/styles/fonts, or it'll break the page) rather than treating `helmet()` as a complete, zero-configuration security solution — it's a strong, well-vetted starting point, not a substitute for the rest of an app's security practices (input validation, auth, dependency hygiene).

questions.question: What is the difference between authentication and authorization, and how would you implement both in an Express application?
questions.answer: Authentication answers 'who are you?' — verifying a user's identity, typically via credentials (password, OAuth, a valid session/token). Authorization answers 'what are you allowed to do?' — given a known, authenticated identity, deciding whether that specific user has permission to perform a specific action or access a specific resource. They're implemented as two distinct, sequential middleware layers in Express: an authentication middleware runs first, verifying a JWT or session and attaching the resolved user (with their roles/permissions) to `req.user`, rejecting the request with `401 Unauthorized` if identity can't be established at all; then an authorization middleware or in-route check runs after, comparing `req.user`'s role/permissions against what the specific route requires, rejecting with `403 Forbidden` if the user is legitimately identified but not permitted to do this particular thing — e.g., `function requireAdmin(req, res, next) { if (req.user.role !== 'admin') return res.status(403).json({ error: 'Forbidden' }); next(); }` applied to admin-only routes after the auth middleware. Keeping these as separate concerns (rather than one big check) makes the codebase easier to reason about and extend — e.g., adding a new role or a more granular permission system later only touches the authorization layer, not identity verification.

questions.question: What is GraphQL, and how does it compare to a REST API in terms of data fetching and over-fetching/under-fetching?
questions.answer: GraphQL is a query language and runtime for APIs where the client specifies exactly what fields and nested relationships it wants in a single request, and the server returns exactly that shape — as opposed to REST, where each endpoint returns a fixed, server-defined response shape, and the client has to accept whatever fields that endpoint includes. This directly addresses two common REST pain points: over-fetching (a REST endpoint returns a full user object with 20 fields when the client only needed the name and avatar, wasting bandwidth) and under-fetching (a screen needs data that spans multiple REST endpoints — a post, its author, and its comments — requiring several sequential round trips or a bespoke aggregation endpoint), both of which GraphQL solves by letting the client request a post plus its author's name plus its comments' text all in one query, resolved server-side in a single round trip. The trade-off: GraphQL pushes more complexity onto the server (resolvers, and the N+1-query risk discussed elsewhere in this bank, since each nested field can trigger its own data fetch unless batched), and its flexible-shape responses make simple HTTP-level caching (which REST gets for free via URLs and standard cache headers) harder — GraphQL typically needs its own caching strategy at the query or field level. In practice, many APIs use REST for straightforward CRUD resources and add GraphQL specifically for complex, client-driven data-fetching needs (e.g., mobile apps needing tightly-tailored payloads).

questions.question: How would you connect a Node.js application to a database, and why is connection pooling important?
questions.answer: You connect via a driver or ORM specific to the database (e.g., `pg` for PostgreSQL, `mongodb`/Mongoose for MongoDB, `mysql2` for MySQL), initializing the connection with credentials typically sourced from environment variables, and reusing that connection object across your application rather than creating and tearing one down per request. Connection pooling matters because establishing a new database connection is relatively expensive — it involves a TCP handshake, authentication, and often TLS negotiation — and doing that fresh for every incoming HTTP request would add meaningful latency to every single request and could quickly exhaust the database's own limit on concurrent connections under load. A connection pool (built into most drivers, e.g. `pg.Pool`) instead maintains a fixed-size set of already-established connections that requests borrow from and return to when done, reusing them instead of paying setup cost repeatedly: `const pool = new Pool({ max: 20 }); const result = await pool.query('SELECT * FROM users WHERE id = $1', [id]);`. Sizing the pool matters — too small and requests queue waiting for a free connection under load; too large and you risk overwhelming the database server itself, since it also has a hard connection limit shared across every app instance connecting to it, which is a real concern when horizontally scaling multiple Node.js instances against the same database.

questions.question: What is a message queue (e.g., RabbitMQ or Kafka), and why would you introduce one into a Node.js-based system?
questions.answer: A message queue is a middleware component that decouples producers (services that emit messages/events) from consumers (services that process them), allowing a producer to fire off a message without waiting for it to be handled synchronously, and letting consumers process at their own pace, independently, and even be scaled or restarted without the producer needing to know or care. You'd introduce one into a Node.js system to: move slow or non-time-critical work (sending emails, generating reports, processing uploaded images) out of the request/response cycle so API latency isn't coupled to that work's duration; add resilience — if a consumer crashes or a downstream service is temporarily down, messages can sit safely in the queue and be retried/redelivered rather than being lost; and enable one event to fan out to multiple independent consumers (order-placed triggers inventory update, email confirmation, and analytics tracking, each handled by a separate consumer) without the producer needing direct knowledge of all of them. RabbitMQ is a traditional message broker built around queues and flexible routing (good for task distribution and RPC-style patterns); Kafka is a distributed, persistent, append-only log built for high-throughput event streaming where multiple consumers can independently replay history — the choice depends on whether you need simple task queuing (RabbitMQ, or in Node specifically a Redis-backed library like BullMQ) versus durable, replayable event streams at scale (Kafka).

questions.question: What are the benefits of using TypeScript in a Node.js project, and what trade-offs come with it?
questions.answer: TypeScript adds a static type system on top of JavaScript, catching a class of bugs (calling a method that doesn't exist on an object, passing the wrong argument type, forgetting to handle `null`/`undefined`) at compile time rather than at runtime in production. In a Node.js backend specifically, this pays off most on larger, longer-lived codebases and teams: it makes refactoring safer (the compiler flags every call site a signature change breaks), it turns your function signatures and data models into enforced, self-documenting contracts (especially valuable across service boundaries or when a large team is working on shared code), and it gives editors much better autocomplete and inline documentation. The trade-offs: it adds a build/compile step (or a transpile-on-the-fly setup) that wasn't previously needed, it has a real learning curve and can slow down initial development velocity on a small or short-lived project, and TypeScript's type system is erased at runtime — a type-safe function can still receive genuinely malformed data from an external API or user input that the compiler had no way to check, so runtime validation (Zod, Joi) is still necessary at your application's actual boundaries. It's worth noting Node.js itself has recently added native TypeScript type-stripping support (running `.ts` files directly without a separate build step for straightforward cases), which has lowered some of the tooling friction historically associated with adopting TypeScript in Node projects.

questions.question: How would you set up a basic CI/CD pipeline for a Node.js application?
questions.answer: A basic pipeline (using something like GitHub Actions, GitLab CI, or CircleCI) triggers on every push/pull request and runs a sequence of automated stages: install dependencies deterministically (`npm ci`, not `npm install`, since `ci` enforces the lockfile exactly and fails fast if it's out of sync — much better suited to a reproducible CI environment); lint (ESLint) to catch style/quality issues; test (unit and integration tests, often against a spun-up test database service in the CI runner) with coverage reporting; and build (TypeScript compilation, bundling, or Docker image creation) if applicable — with the pipeline failing fast at whichever stage first fails, blocking the PR from being merged. The CD (continuous deployment/delivery) half then takes a build that passed all of the above and automatically deploys it — often gated by branch (merges to `main` auto-deploy to staging, a tagged release or manual approval deploys to production), commonly using a strategy like rolling deployment or blue-green to avoid downtime, paired with automated smoke tests or health-check verification post-deploy, and an easy rollback path if something goes wrong. The key principle interviewers look for: every stage should be automated and required to pass before code reaches production, removing manual, error-prone gatekeeping from the release process.

questions.question: How would you containerize a Node.js application with Docker, and what should you keep in mind for image size and security?
questions.answer: A basic `Dockerfile` starts from an official Node base image, copies `package.json`/`package-lock.json` first and runs `npm ci` before copying the rest of the source code — ordering it this way lets Docker's layer caching skip the (often slow) dependency install step on rebuilds where only application code changed, not dependencies. For image size and security, several practices matter: use a multi-stage build — compile/build in one stage (with dev dependencies and build tools present) and copy only the resulting build artifacts and production dependencies into a slim final stage, so the shipped image doesn't carry TypeScript, test frameworks, or build tooling; prefer a minimal base image (`node:20-alpine` or a `-slim` variant) over the full default image to shrink attack surface and download size; run `npm ci --omit=dev` in the final stage so `devDependencies` aren't shipped to production at all; and explicitly run the container as a non-root user (most official Node images include a pre-created `node` user for exactly this purpose) rather than the default root, so a container compromise doesn't automatically grant root inside the container. It's also worth using a `.dockerignore` file (excluding `node_modules`, `.git`, `.env`) to avoid accidentally baking local artifacts or secrets into the image, and scanning the final image for known vulnerabilities (e.g., with `docker scan` or Trivy) as part of CI.

questions.question: What is the difference between a monolithic architecture and a microservices architecture, and what are the trade-offs for a Node.js-based system?
questions.answer: A monolith is a single deployable application containing all of a system's functionality — one codebase, one build, one deployment, typically one database — where different modules communicate via in-process function calls. Microservices split that functionality into multiple independently deployable services, each owning its own data and communicating over the network (HTTP/REST, gRPC, or message queues), each of which can be built, deployed, scaled, and even written in a different language independently of the others. For a Node.js system specifically, a monolith is usually the right starting point for a new product — it's simpler to develop, test, deploy, and debug (one process, one log stream, no network calls between your own components), and Node's single-threaded model combined with `cluster`/multiple instances already gives you meaningful horizontal scaling without needing to split the codebase. Microservices become worth the added complexity once you hit real organizational or scaling pressure: multiple teams needing to deploy independently without blocking each other, different parts of the system having wildly different scaling or resource needs (a CPU-heavy image-processing service versus a lightweight CRUD API), or a genuine need for technology diversity. The cost is real, though: distributed systems complexity (network failures, partial failures, eventual consistency between services' data), more sophisticated observability requirements (distributed tracing becomes necessary, not optional), and significantly more operational overhead (service discovery, more deployment pipelines, inter-service auth) — which is why 'start with a monolith, split out services only when you have a concrete, evidenced reason to' is common, mainstream architectural advice rather than defaulting to microservices from day one.

questions.question: How would you implement a simple in-memory or Redis-based caching layer in a Node.js application?
questions.answer: An in-memory cache (a plain `Map`, or a purpose-built library like `lru-cache` for automatic eviction/TTL support) keeps recently-fetched or expensive-to-compute data directly in your Node process's memory: `const cache = new LRUCache({ max: 500, ttl: 60000 }); async function getUser(id) { if (cache.has(id)) return cache.get(id); const user = await db.findUser(id); cache.set(id, user); return user; }`. This is the fastest possible cache (no network hop) but has two important limits: it's bound by process memory (hence needing an eviction policy like LRU rather than growing unbounded), and it's per-instance — if you're running multiple Node.js instances (via `cluster` or multiple containers), each has its own separate, inconsistent in-memory cache. A Redis-based cache solves that by centralizing the cache in a separate, shared service every instance talks to over the network — `await redisClient.set(key, JSON.stringify(user), { EX: 60 })` to cache with a 60-second expiry, `await redisClient.get(key)` to read — trading a small network round trip for consistency across all your app instances, plus the ability to survive individual instance restarts (the cache itself doesn't reset just because one app process did). Cache invalidation is the genuinely hard part in both cases: deciding when a cached value becomes stale and needs to be evicted or refreshed (TTL-based expiry, explicit invalidation on writes, or a cache-aside pattern) is where most real-world caching bugs come from.

questions.question: What is the reactor pattern, and how does it relate to how Node.js handles concurrent I/O?
questions.answer: The reactor pattern is a design pattern for handling concurrent service requests using a single (or small number of) thread(s): instead of dedicating a thread per connection/request (as many traditional server architectures do), a reactor registers interest in events (like 'this socket has data ready to read') with a demultiplexer, and when the underlying OS signals that an event has occurred, the reactor dispatches it to the appropriate registered handler/callback, which runs to completion before the reactor goes back to waiting for the next event. This is exactly the architecture Node.js is built on: libuv acts as the event demultiplexer, using OS-native mechanisms (epoll/kqueue/IOCP) to efficiently watch many file descriptors/sockets at once without blocking, and the Node.js event loop is the reactor that pulls ready events off that demultiplexer and invokes the JavaScript callbacks associated with them, one at a time, on the single main thread. This is precisely why Node.js can handle thousands of concurrent connections with a single thread without a thread-per-connection model: the thread is never blocked waiting on any individual I/O operation — it's just reacting to whichever operation becomes ready next — and true parallelism for the actual OS-level I/O work happens underneath, in the kernel or libuv's thread pool, not in application-visible JavaScript threads.

questions.question: What is the difference between scaling with Node's Cluster module on one machine versus running multiple instances behind an external load balancer?
questions.answer: The `cluster` module scales within a single machine: a primary process forks one worker process per CPU core, all sharing a listening port, giving you multi-core utilization on that one host with a relatively simple setup — the primary itself handles distributing connections to workers. Running multiple instances behind an external load balancer (an actual reverse proxy or cloud load balancer like Nginx, HAProxy, or an AWS ALB) scales across machines/containers — you run N independent Node.js processes, potentially on entirely different physical or virtual hosts, and the load balancer sits in front of all of them, routing incoming traffic across whichever instances are healthy. In practice these aren't mutually exclusive — a common production setup uses both together: each machine/container runs a clustered Node.js process to use all of its own cores, and a load balancer sits in front of multiple such machines/containers to scale horizontally beyond what any single box could handle, and to provide the resilience benefit of surviving an entire machine going down (something the `cluster` module alone, confined to one host, can't protect against). The external-load-balancer approach also decouples scaling from any single machine's core count and works naturally with container orchestration (Kubernetes horizontal pod autoscaling, for example), whereas `cluster` scaling is capped by the number of cores on the box it's running on.

questions.question: What is util.promisify() used for, and when would you reach for it?
questions.answer: `util.promisify()`, from Node's core `node:util` module, takes a function following the traditional Node error-first callback style — `fn(arg1, ..., callback)` where `callback` is `(err, result) => {}` — and returns a new function that instead returns a Promise, resolving with the result or rejecting with the error. This is useful for working with older, callback-based core APIs or third-party libraries inside modern `async/await` code without manually wrapping each call in a `new Promise((resolve, reject) => {...})`: `const stat = util.promisify(fs.stat); const stats = await stat('.');` — much cleaner than nesting the callback manually. A documented gotcha worth knowing for an interview: `promisify()` assumes the callback is the last argument and follows the strict error-first convention, so it won't work correctly on functions that don't follow that exact pattern (some APIs, notably `fs.exists`, historically didn't and needed special-casing or avoidance). Another real gotcha, called out directly in Node's own docs: promisifying a method that internally relies on `this` (e.g., a class method) can break unless you `.bind()` it to the right object first, since `promisify()` doesn't preserve the calling context automatically. In modern code, this is used less than it once was, since many core modules and popular libraries now expose Promise-based APIs directly (e.g., `require('node:fs/promises')`), but it's still valuable glue when integrating with legacy callback-style code.

questions.question: What is the difference between the net module and the dgram module in Node.js?
questions.answer: `node:net` provides an API for working with TCP (and Unix domain socket) servers and clients — TCP is connection-oriented and reliable: it establishes a handshake, guarantees in-order delivery, and automatically retransmits lost packets, at the cost of some overhead. `net.createServer()` gives you a TCP server you can listen on, and `net.Socket` represents an individual TCP connection you can read from and write to as a stream. `node:dgram` provides an API for UDP, which is connectionless and unreliable by design: there's no handshake, no guarantee packets arrive, arrive only once, or arrive in order — but that also means there's no connection-setup latency and no head-of-line blocking, since each datagram is independent. In practice: use `net` (or higher-level protocols built on it, like `http`/`https`) for anything needing reliable, ordered delivery — most application-level networking, including virtually all web APIs — and reach for `dgram` when you specifically need low-latency, best-effort delivery and can tolerate occasional loss or reordering at the application level, such as real-time video/audio streaming, certain gaming protocols, DNS-style query/response exchanges, or service discovery via multicast — cases where retransmitting a late packet is worse than simply dropping it and moving on.

questions.question: What are the key differences between Bun, Deno, and Node.js as JavaScript runtimes?
questions.answer: All three run server-side JavaScript/TypeScript but differ in engine and philosophy. Node.js runs on V8 and remains, as of 2026, the dominant default for production due to its maturity, the largest and most battle-tested package ecosystem via npm, and the widest range of deployment tooling and operational familiarity across the industry — its trade-offs are comparatively slower installs/cold starts and a historically more fragmented CommonJS/ESM story (though this has continued to improve). Deno, created by Node's original author specifically to address design regrets in Node, also runs on V8 but ships with native TypeScript support with no separate build step, a secure-by-default permission model (scripts have no filesystem/network/env access unless explicitly granted, unlike Node's unrestricted-by-default model), and a URL-based module system; Deno 2 added substantial Node.js/npm compatibility, closing much of what was previously its biggest adoption gap. Bun runs on JavaScriptCore (Safari's engine, not V8) and is built specifically around speed — dramatically faster package installs and generally faster raw execution/startup in benchmarks — while also bundling a package manager, bundler, and test runner into a single binary, aiming to be a largely drop-in, Node-API-compatible replacement. The practical, non-hype-driven guidance across most 2026 sources: Node remains the safe default for existing/enterprise production systems given its ecosystem maturity and operational track record; Bun is compelling for new, performance-sensitive projects willing to accept a still-smaller Bun-specific ecosystem; Deno suits teams prioritizing security isolation, native TypeScript, or edge deployment. Benchmark numbers across sources vary significantly by workload (I/O-bound workloads narrow the gap between runtimes substantially compared to CPU-bound microbenchmarks), so it's worth treating specific throughput figures skeptically without testing your own workload.

questions.question: How would you implement internationalization (i18n) in a Node.js application?
questions.answer: Internationalization (i18n) means structuring an application so it can be adapted to different languages/locales without code changes, while localization (l10n) is the actual process of providing translations for a given language. In a Node.js backend, the standard approach is to externalize all user-facing strings into locale-specific resource files rather than hardcoding them (e.g., `en.json`, `es.json`, each mapping keys to translated strings), then use a library like `i18next` (commonly paired with `i18next-http-middleware` in an Express app) to detect the requesting user's preferred locale — typically from an `Accept-Language` header, a query parameter, or a stored user preference — and look up strings by key against the appropriate locale file at request time: `res.__('welcome_message')` or `i18next.t('welcome_message', { lng: detectedLocale })`. Beyond just string translation, proper i18n also needs to account for locale-sensitive formatting of dates, numbers, and currency (JavaScript's built-in `Intl` API — `Intl.DateTimeFormat`, `Intl.NumberFormat` — handles this natively without extra dependencies), and pluralization rules, which differ non-trivially across languages (some languages have more than the English two plural forms) — a reason dedicated i18n libraries are generally preferred over naive string substitution for anything beyond a single-language app.

questions.question: What is Server-Side Rendering (SSR), and why might you use it in a Node.js-based application?
questions.answer: Server-Side Rendering means generating the full HTML markup for a page on the server, for each request, and sending that fully-formed HTML to the browser — as opposed to Client-Side Rendering (CSR), where the server sends a mostly-empty HTML shell plus a JavaScript bundle, and the browser itself builds the actual page content after the JS loads and runs. Node.js is a natural fit for SSR of JavaScript-framework applications (React, Vue, etc.) because the same language/ecosystem used for the frontend components can also run on the server to render them to HTML strings — frameworks like Next.js (React) and Nuxt (Vue) are built specifically around this. You'd reach for SSR primarily for: SEO — search engine crawlers (and social media link-preview scrapers) historically parse and index initial HTML much more reliably than they execute client-side JavaScript, so content that needs to be discoverable benefits from arriving pre-rendered; and perceived performance — the user sees meaningful content sooner (faster First Contentful Paint), since they aren't waiting for a JS bundle to download, parse, and execute before anything appears on screen, which matters especially on slower networks/devices. The trade-off is added server load (rendering work now happens per-request on your servers instead of being offloaded entirely to the client) and additional architectural complexity (hydration — attaching client-side interactivity to server-rendered markup — can introduce its own class of bugs if server and client render mismatched output).

questions.question: How does the V8 garbage collector work in Node.js, and what are the generational GC phases (Scavenge, Mark-Sweep, Mark-Compact)?
questions.answer: V8's garbage collector (codenamed Orinoco) is generational, based on the empirical 'generational hypothesis' that most objects die young. Per V8's own engineering blog, the heap is split into a young generation (further divided into a 'nursery' and an 'intermediate' sub-generation) and an old generation; new objects are always allocated into the nursery first. The young generation is collected by the Scavenger (a Minor GC), using Cheney's semispace copying algorithm: the young generation is split into an active 'from-space' and an empty 'to-space', and during a scavenge, still-reachable objects are copied from from-space into to-space (objects surviving their second scavenge get promoted into the old generation instead), after which from-space is entirely garbage and gets reused as the next to-space — this makes the young generation fast to collect precisely because it never has to trace unreachable objects, only copy the (typically much smaller) set of survivors. The old generation is collected by the Major GC, using Mark-Sweep-Compact: a mark phase traces the object graph from GC roots to identify everything still reachable (using a tri-color marking scheme — white/grey/black — to track progress), a sweep phase reclaims memory from unmarked (garbage) objects, and, for pages that have become too fragmented, a compact phase additionally moves surviving objects together to eliminate fragmentation and allow larger contiguous future allocations — sweep-only is used on less-fragmented pages since compaction (copying live objects) is comparatively more expensive. Because Major GC on a large old-generation heap could otherwise cause a long, visible pause ('stop-the-world'), V8 has invested heavily in making much of this work parallel (multiple helper threads sharing the marking/compaction work), concurrent (running alongside live JavaScript execution on background threads rather than pausing it), and incremental (breaking the work into small slices interleaved with normal execution) — this is the core of what the 'Orinoco' project actually shipped.

questions.question: How does V8's JIT compilation pipeline optimize JavaScript execution over the lifetime of a running process?
questions.answer: Per V8's own blog, modern V8 uses a multi-tiered pipeline rather than a single compiler, trading off compilation speed against generated-code quality at each tier. All JavaScript is first parsed and compiled to bytecode executed by Ignition, V8's interpreter — this gets code running with minimal startup delay, and critically, while interpreting, V8 collects runtime feedback about how the code actually behaves (which object 'shapes'/hidden classes flow through a given call site, which branches are taken, argument types seen). If a function is called often enough ('warm'), it's promoted to Sparkplug, a genuinely non-optimizing baseline JIT (introduced 2021) that compiles Ignition's bytecode almost 1:1 into real machine code in microseconds, eliminating interpreter dispatch overhead without spending time on speculative optimization. Functions that stay hot longer get promoted further to Maglev (introduced 2023), a mid-tier optimizing compiler that builds on the type feedback already gathered to generate meaningfully faster code than Sparkplug, but compiles much faster than the top tier. The hottest, longest-running functions eventually reach TurboFan, V8's peak optimizing compiler, which spends significantly more compile time generating highly specialized machine code based on speculative assumptions from the accumulated feedback (e.g., 'this object always has this exact shape,' 'this variable is always a small integer'). The critical safety mechanism tying this together is deoptimization: if a TurboFan- or Maglev-optimized function's speculative assumptions are ever violated at runtime (e.g., a previously-integer-only variable suddenly receives a string), execution immediately bails back down to Ignition to run safely and correctly, and V8 may re-collect feedback and re-optimize later — this tiered, feedback-driven, speculate-and-deoptimize architecture is what lets V8 deliver both fast startup and near-native peak performance for genuinely hot code, without needing to statically prove type safety the way an ahead-of-time compiled language would.

questions.question: How would you design rate limiting using the token bucket, leaky bucket, and sliding window algorithms, and when would you choose each?
questions.answer: Token bucket: a bucket holds up to a fixed capacity of tokens, refilled at a steady rate; each incoming request consumes one token, and a request is allowed only if a token is available — if the bucket is empty, the request is rejected/delayed. Its key property is that it naturally allows short bursts up to the bucket's capacity (a client that's been quiet can suddenly send a burst as long as tokens have accumulated), which makes it a good fit for APIs where occasional legitimate bursts (a page load firing several requests at once) shouldn't be unfairly punished. Leaky bucket: requests are queued and processed (leak out) at a strictly constant rate regardless of how bursty the incoming traffic is — if the queue fills up faster than it drains, excess requests are dropped. This enforces a smooth, constant output rate, making it well-suited to protecting a downstream system that genuinely can't handle bursts at all (e.g., a fixed-capacity resource behind it), at the cost of added latency for anything queued. Sliding window (log or counter variant) counts requests within a continuously moving time window (e.g., 'the last 60 seconds, recalculated on every request') rather than a fixed window that resets at a boundary — this avoids the classic fixed-window flaw where a client could send its full quota right at the end of one window and again immediately at the start of the next, effectively doubling the intended rate in a short burst around the boundary. In practice: reach for token bucket when you want to permit reasonable burstiness (most general-purpose public API rate limiting, e.g. `express-rate-limit`'s default algorithm is closer to fixed/sliding window, while cloud API gateways like AWS API Gateway explicitly use token bucket); leaky bucket when you need a hard, smooth output ceiling protecting a fragile downstream dependency; and sliding window when precise, boundary-exploit-resistant rate accuracy matters more than implementation simplicity.

questions.question: How would you design inter-service communication in a Node.js microservices architecture, and what are the trade-offs between REST, message queues, and gRPC?
questions.answer: The right choice depends on whether the interaction is synchronous request/response, needs guaranteed delivery/decoupling, or is latency/throughput-critical. REST over HTTP is the simplest and most broadly compatible option — human-readable, easy to debug, works with standard HTTP tooling and infrastructure (load balancers, caches, API gateways) out of the box — making it a reasonable default for synchronous service-to-service calls where simplicity and interoperability matter more than raw performance, but it carries per-request JSON serialization overhead and creates temporal coupling: the calling service blocks waiting on the response, and if the callee is down, the call fails immediately unless you add your own retry/circuit-breaker logic. Message queues (RabbitMQ, Kafka, or Redis-backed queues like BullMQ) decouple services entirely in time — a producer publishes an event/task without waiting for a consumer to process it, consumers can be down temporarily without losing work (assuming persistent queues), and one event can fan out to multiple independent consumers — the right choice for asynchronous workflows (order placed → inventory, billing, and notification services each react independently) where the caller genuinely doesn't need an immediate response. gRPC uses Protocol Buffers (a compact binary serialization format) over HTTP/2, giving significantly lower serialization overhead and latency than JSON-over-HTTP/1.1, strongly-typed contracts generated from a shared `.proto` schema (catching mismatches at compile time rather than runtime), and native support for streaming (bidirectional, not just request/response) — trade-offs are reduced human-readability/debuggability compared to REST, less mature browser support (typically requires a proxy like grpc-web for browser clients), and a steeper learning curve. A common real-world pattern: gRPC or REST for synchronous, latency-sensitive internal service-to-service calls; message queues for asynchronous, fire-and-forget or fan-out workflows; and REST/GraphQL at the public-facing edge for broad client compatibility.

questions.question: How would you implement distributed request tracing across multiple Node.js microservices using OpenTelemetry?
questions.answer: The core idea of distributed tracing is following a single logical request as it flows across multiple services, so you can see the full picture — which services were called, in what order, how long each took, and where a failure or slowdown actually occurred — rather than only seeing each service's logs in isolation. OpenTelemetry is the current, vendor-neutral standard for this: you instrument each Node.js service with the OpenTelemetry SDK (either auto-instrumentation packages that hook into common libraries like `http`, Express, and popular database clients with no code changes, or manual instrumentation for custom logic), which generates spans — each representing one unit of work (an incoming HTTP request, an outgoing call to another service, a database query) — with a start/end time and metadata. The critical mechanism that ties spans together across service boundaries is context propagation: when Service A calls Service B, OpenTelemetry injects a trace context (a `traceparent` header, per the W3C Trace Context standard) into the outgoing request, carrying the trace ID and the calling span's ID; Service B's instrumentation extracts that header and creates its own span as a child of A's span, rather than starting a brand-new, disconnected trace — this is exactly the kind of cross-async-boundary context propagation that Node's `AsyncLocalStorage` is used internally to implement, since a request's tracing context has to survive through however many `await`s and callbacks the request handling involves. All the spans generated across every service, sharing the same trace ID, are exported to a backend (Jaeger, Tempo, or a commercial APM) that reassembles them into a single visual timeline (a 'waterfall' or flame-graph-style view) of the entire distributed request, letting you pinpoint exactly which downstream call was the slow one or where an error was first introduced.

questions.question: How would you scale WebSocket connections across multiple Node.js server instances (e.g., using Redis pub/sub)?
questions.answer: A single Node.js instance can hold many WebSocket connections in memory, but once you run multiple instances behind a load balancer for scale or redundancy, a new problem appears: each instance only knows about the WebSocket clients directly connected to it — if a message needs to reach a client connected to a different instance (e.g., a chat message needs to reach a recipient who happens to be connected to instance B, but was generated by a handler running on instance A), that instance has no direct way to deliver it. The standard solution is to introduce a shared message broker — commonly Redis pub/sub — as a fan-out layer between instances: when any instance needs to broadcast a message, instead of trying to send it directly to sockets it doesn't own, it publishes the message to a Redis channel; every instance subscribes to that same channel, and each one checks whether any of its own locally-connected clients should receive that message, delivering it locally if so. In practice, this is rarely hand-rolled — Socket.IO ships a `@socket.io/redis-adapter` that implements exactly this pattern transparently, so `io.emit()` or room-based broadcasts work correctly across a cluster of instances without the application code needing to know how many instances exist. A related, often-overlooked requirement: because WebSocket connections are long-lived and stateful, the load balancer in front of the instances needs sticky sessions (or the WebSocket handshake needs to be routed consistently to the same instance for that connection's lifetime) — an ordinary round-robin load balancer that could route a reconnect attempt to a different instance mid-session will break naive assumptions about connection state, which is one reason the pub/sub fan-out approach (rather than relying on connections always landing on the 'right' instance) is the more robust pattern.

questions.question: What are the trade-offs of adopting a serverless architecture for a Node.js application, and how do cold starts affect your design decisions?
questions.answer: Serverless (e.g., AWS Lambda, Google Cloud Functions running Node.js) trades operational control for reduced operational burden: you deploy individual functions rather than managing servers, scaling happens automatically and near-instantly in response to load, and you pay per invocation/execution time rather than for idle server capacity — genuinely compelling for spiky, unpredictable, or low-average-but-high-peak workloads (webhooks, scheduled jobs, event-driven processing) where provisioning fixed server capacity would mean paying for a lot of idle time. The major, defining downside is the cold start: when a function hasn't been invoked recently, the platform has to provision a fresh execution environment — starting the Node.js runtime, loading your code and its dependencies, running any module-level initialization — before your handler code can even begin executing, adding real, user-visible latency (often ranging from tens of milliseconds to well over a second, depending on runtime, package size, and platform) to that particular request; subsequent requests hitting an already-'warm' instance skip this entirely. This directly shapes how you design a Node.js serverless function: minimize dependencies and bundle size (fewer/smaller `node_modules` to load), avoid heavy work in module-level (outside-the-handler) code unless it's something you specifically want to run once per cold environment and reuse across warm invocations (like a database connection, which should be created outside the handler so it can be reused on subsequent warm invocations rather than reconnected every single call), and consider a platform's 'provisioned concurrency' or equivalent (pre-warmed instances kept ready, at extra cost) for latency-sensitive endpoints where cold starts are unacceptable. Other trade-offs worth mentioning: a hard execution time limit per invocation (unsuitable for long-running tasks), vendor lock-in risk around the specific serverless platform's APIs/event formats, and harder local development/debugging compared to a normal long-running server process.

questions.question: How would you detect and mitigate a DDoS attack against a Node.js-based HTTP server?
questions.answer: Detection starts with monitoring for the tell-tale signatures: a sudden, sharp spike in request rate (often from many distinct IPs simultaneously, distinguishing a distributed attack from one misbehaving client), a disproportionate share of traffic hitting a small number of expensive endpoints, unusual patterns like identical or near-identical request payloads/user-agents at high volume, or a spike in event loop lag/CPU/connection counts without a corresponding legitimate traffic increase — this is why baseline metrics (normal request rate, latency percentiles, connection counts) matter, since you can't detect an anomaly without knowing what normal looks like. Mitigation is layered, and a well-designed Node.js application generally shouldn't be the first line of defense: the most effective protection sits in front of the application entirely — a CDN or dedicated DDoS-protection service (Cloudflare, AWS Shield) that absorbs and filters volumetric attacks before they ever reach your infrastructure, since a sufficiently large volumetric attack can saturate network bandwidth in ways no application-level code can meaningfully defend against. At the application/infrastructure layer beneath that: rate limiting (per-IP or per-API-key, ideally backed by a shared store like Redis so it works correctly across multiple instances) to cap how much any single source can consume; connection/request timeouts and limits on header size and body size to prevent slow-loris-style attacks that tie up connections with minimal actual data; a Web Application Firewall (WAF) rule set to filter obviously malicious patterns before they hit application code; and ensuring the application itself doesn't have accidentally-expensive endpoints that amplify a small number of requests into disproportionate backend load (e.g., an unauthenticated search endpoint that triggers a full, unindexed table scan). The overarching principle for a Node.js-specific angle: because a single blocking, expensive operation can stall the entire event loop for every user, auditing for and eliminating accidentally-blocking or unbounded-cost code paths is itself a meaningful DDoS-resilience measure, not just a general performance concern.

questions.question: How would you design a robust global error-handling strategy for uncaught exceptions and unhandled promise rejections in a production Node.js service?
questions.answer: The first principle: `process.on('uncaughtException', ...)` and `process.on('unhandledRejection', ...)` are safety nets for logging and controlled shutdown, never a substitute for actually handling errors correctly at their source (try/catch around awaits, `.catch()` on promise chains, error-handling Express middleware). Per Node's own documentation, an uncaught synchronous exception leaves the process in a potentially corrupted, unknown state — the official guidance is that the correct response is to log full diagnostic detail and then let the process exit, rather than trying to 'recover' and keep serving traffic from a process whose in-memory state integrity can no longer be trusted. For unhandled promise rejections specifically, it's important to know that Node's default `--unhandled-rejections` mode is `throw` — meaning an unhandled rejection is escalated to an uncaught exception and crashes the process by default in modern Node versions, which is a meaningful behavior change from older Node versions that merely printed a warning and kept running. A solid production strategy: register both handlers to log the full error (including stack trace and any request-correlation ID, ideally via `AsyncLocalStorage`-based context) to your monitoring/APM system (Sentry, Datadog, etc.) before exiting, then call `process.exit(1)` deliberately rather than letting the process linger in a possibly-corrupted state; pair this with a process manager or container orchestrator (PM2, Kubernetes) configured to automatically restart the crashed process, so a single bad request causes a brief, contained restart rather than an ongoing outage; and, for anything in a `cluster` setup, ensure the primary process detects a worker's exit and forks a replacement so overall capacity is maintained. It's also worth explicitly separating this global safety net from your application's everyday, expected-error handling (like a `404` for a missing resource or a `400` for bad input) — those should never reach `uncaughtException` at all; that handler exists specifically for genuinely unexpected programming errors and bugs.

questions.question: What are the performance trade-offs of using async/await versus raw Promise chains in hot code paths?
questions.answer: Functionally, `async/await` is syntactic sugar over Promises — an `async` function always returns a Promise, and `await` is roughly equivalent to chaining a `.then()` — so in the vast majority of application code, the difference is readability and error-handling ergonomics (as covered elsewhere in this bank), not a meaningful performance gap; modern V8 has invested significant optimization work specifically into making `async/await` fast, closing what used to be a more noticeable historical gap between the two styles in older engine versions. Where a genuine difference can show up in extremely hot, high-iteration code paths: each `await` introduces a microtask-queue tick, meaning a long chain of sequential `await`s (each depending on the last) forces the event loop to yield back to the microtask queue at every step, which — in a tight loop executed millions of times — can add up to measurably more overhead than a single, carefully constructed `.then()` chain or, more importantly, than restructuring the code to avoid unnecessary sequential awaiting entirely. The much more impactful, commonly-tested mistake in this area isn't `async/await` vs `.then()` at all — it's writing code that `await`s several independent operations sequentially inside a loop (`for (const id of ids) { results.push(await fetchItem(id)); }`) when those operations don't actually depend on each other and could run concurrently via `Promise.all(ids.map(fetchItem))`, which is very often a 10x+ real-world performance difference and matters far more than the micro-level cost of `await` itself. The practical interview takeaway: don't optimize `async/await` vs `.then()` syntax choice for performance — optimize for whether your async operations are actually being run concurrently when they safely could be, since that's where the real cost usually hides.

questions.question: How would you design a connection-pooling strategy for a Node.js service under heavy database load?
questions.answer: The central tension is that a pool needs to be large enough to serve concurrent request load without requests queuing for a free connection, but small enough not to overwhelm the database — which has its own hard connection limit, often shared across every instance of your application connecting to it simultaneously, not just one. Sizing should start from the database's actual capacity, not an arbitrary per-app number: if the database can safely sustain, say, 200 concurrent connections total, and you run 10 horizontally-scaled Node.js instances, each instance's pool should be sized with that shared ceiling in mind (roughly 20 each, with headroom), not each independently defaulting to some larger number that collectively overshoots the database's limit under simultaneous peak load across all instances. Beyond raw sizing: set a reasonable connection acquisition timeout, so a request that can't get a pooled connection within a bounded time fails fast with a clear error rather than hanging indefinitely and tying up the request-handling thread; configure idle-connection eviction so connections that have sat unused for too long are recycled rather than held open indefinitely (some databases/proxies also silently drop long-idle connections server-side, so the pool needs to detect and replace dead connections gracefully rather than handing out a broken one); and monitor pool utilization (active vs idle vs queued-waiters) as a first-class production metric, since a pool that's frequently saturated is a leading indicator of either genuine capacity pressure or a slow-query problem making connections held longer than they should be. For very high load scenarios beyond what direct pooling can handle, introducing an external connection pooler/proxy (like PgBouncer for PostgreSQL) in front of the database lets you multiplex a much larger number of application-level logical connections onto a smaller number of actual database connections, decoupling the two scaling concerns.

questions.question: How would you use CPU profiling (e.g., --prof, Clinic.js, flame graphs) to find and fix a performance hotspot in a Node.js service?
questions.answer: CPU profiling samples what the JavaScript engine is actually executing at regular intervals over a period of load, building up a picture of where time is being spent across your call stack — the goal is to replace guessing about what's slow with actual, measured evidence. Node's built-in `--prof` flag (`node --prof server.js`, then generating load against it) produces a V8 log file that can be processed with `node --prof-process isolate-*.log > processed.txt` into a human-readable summary of time spent in different functions, though it's fairly low-level output. A more ergonomic path for most teams is Clinic.js (specifically Clinic Flame), which wraps this profiling process and, critically, renders the result as a flame graph — a visualization where each horizontal bar is a function call, its width proportional to the time it (and everything it called) consumed, and stacking shows the call hierarchy — making it visually obvious which functions are the widest (most expensive) bars, especially ones that are unexpectedly wide for what they conceptually do. The workflow: generate realistic load against the profiled process (an idle process produces an uninformative profile), capture the profile, then read the flame graph top-down looking for unusually wide frames — common culprits found this way include unnecessarily expensive JSON serialization/parsing of large payloads, inefficient synchronous loops or algorithms with poor complexity, unindexed/expensive database calls masquerading as 'CPU time' if they're synchronous-appearing in the trace, or unexpected garbage collection overhead (visible as time attributed to V8's internal GC functions) pointing back toward a memory-churn problem. Once the hot function is identified, the fix is specific to what it's doing — algorithmic optimization, caching a repeated expensive computation, moving genuinely CPU-bound work to a `worker_threads` pool so it stops monopolizing the main event loop thread — and the same profiling process should be re-run afterward to confirm the fix actually narrowed that bar rather than just moving the bottleneck somewhere else.

questions.question: How would you diagnose a Node.js process that crashes intermittently in production with no clear application-level stack trace (e.g., native addon fault, OOM kill)?
questions.answer: The first, crucial step is distinguishing what kind of crash this actually is, because a JavaScript-level error (which produces a normal stack trace you can act on directly) is a fundamentally different investigation than a crash below the JavaScript layer — and the exit code is the fastest signal: exit code 137 specifically indicates the process was killed by the Linux OOM killer (SIGKILL, signal 9) because the container/host ran out of available memory, while exit code 139 indicates SIGSEGV — a segmentation fault, typically originating from a bug in a native addon or in V8/Node's own C++ layer, accessing memory it shouldn't. For a suspected OOM kill, check the container/host memory limit against actual observed memory usage leading up to the crash (via metrics you should already have from your monitoring stack, or `dmesg`/`journalctl` on the host, which logs OOM killer events explicitly) — the fix path converges with ordinary memory-leak diagnosis (heap snapshots, checking for unbounded caches/listeners), but the memory limit itself may also simply need raising if usage is legitimate rather than leaking. For a suspected segfault/native crash, since Node.js will typically just exit with 'Segmentation fault (core dumped)' and no JavaScript stack trace at all — because the fault occurred in C/C++ code, not JS — the diagnostic path is different: enable core dump generation (`ulimit -c unlimited`) so the next crash produces an analyzable core file, then inspect it with a debugger like `gdb` or the Node-specific `llnode` plugin to get a native (C++) stack trace pointing at the actual faulting library/function; alternatively, a purpose-built tool like `segfault-handler` can be installed proactively to catch `SIGSEGV` and print a native stack trace to a log file at the moment of the crash, without needing a full offline core-dump analysis workflow. In either case, the practical next steps are the same: identify which native addon (if any) is involved, check for known issues or version incompatibilities with your current Node.js version (native addons are especially prone to breaking across Node major-version upgrades unless built against a stable ABI like Node-API), and consider whether that native dependency can be updated, replaced, or isolated (e.g., run in a separate worker process) so a fault in it doesn't take down the entire service.
